paras: The mob attack on William Jackson in the Tenderloin took place on the afternoon of 1 March 1903 on Seventh Avenue in Manhattan, New York, when a crowd of white boys and young men chased and beat Jackson, a Black man, after he tried to stop them tormenting an elderly Black man. Police drove the crowd back and arrested Charles Staub, whom Jackson named as the ringleader, on a charge of disorderly conduct. Two New York papers headlined the episode as a near "race riot" and a "little race war."

According to the Sun, about a dozen white boys gathered at Seventh Avenue and Thirtieth Street, within half a block of the Tenderloin police station, with a long rope. Whenever a Black man came along they took hold of the rope, surrounded him and sang and danced around him, and the Sun said a dozen or more men were annoyed in this way. The Tribune described the group as "the gang of ruffians who hang around Seventh-ave. and Twenty-seventh-st." and said they also used the rope to trip unsuspecting passers-by.

Their last victim was an old Black man, whom the Tribune put at "sixty-five or seventy" and whose arms and legs, it said, were twisted tight in the rope coils. William Jackson, a Black man who lived at 227 West Thirty-second Street, went to his aid, and the tormentors turned on him. In the Sun's account Jackson fought back for a few minutes as the crowd struck and kicked at him, then ran.

The crowd grew as it pursued him up Seventh Avenue; the Sun counted "fully fifty men and boys" by Thirty-first Street and reported yells of "lynch him." The Tribune said the pursuers beat Jackson over the head and back with sticks, small stones and rope ends. The two papers differ on the rescue: the Tribune had Policemen Gilligan and Quinn of the West Thirtieth Street station beating back the crowd with night sticks at Thirtieth Street, while the Sun had Jackson run into the arms of Detective Quinn at Thirty-second Street. The Tribune added that Black residents along that stretch of Seventh Avenue had seen the attack and were "swarming out into the street" to defend Jackson when the police arrived.

Jackson pointed out Charles Staub, eighteen years old, of West Twenty-sixth Street, as the ringleader, and Staub was locked up on a charge of disorderly conduct. The Tribune reported that about an hour later the same gang rescued a young man arrested by an off-duty policeman, Lane, near Seventh Avenue and Twenty-sixth Street, and beat Lane in the gutter. No report of the outcome of Staub's case or of the extent of Jackson's injuries was found.

The episode appeared in two Manhattan dailies on 2 March 1903, each in its own wording. The Tribune ran it on its front page as "Almost a Race Riot," with the deck "Ruffians Assault Negroes," and called the attackers "ruffians" throughout. The Sun's headline, "Boys Start a Little Race War," treated the affair more lightly as boys' mischief, though its text called the pursuers "rowdies" and "loafers."

On 29 March the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic in Arkansas printed an editorial paragraph about a New York fight in which a Black man "bested the white man" and a white mob cried "Lynch the nigger!" before police rescued him. The paragraph named no one and may describe a different incident, but it used the scene to mock the North's professed sympathy "for the negro of the south." No Black-press coverage of the attack was found.

bases: A crowd of white boys and young men chased, struck and kicked a Black man who had intervened for an old man they were tormenting, until police drove them back; no one was killed (A1, A2).

Two separate New York reports with different wording and details (the Tribune and the Sun) agree on the rope-gang tormenting of Black passers-by, the chase and beating of William Jackson, police intervention and Charles Staub's arrest (A1, A2).

accounts.label: New-York Tribune
accounts.gist: A gang of ruffians from Seventh Avenue and Twenty-seventh Street tied an aged Black man in a rope, then chased Jackson to Thirtieth Street and beat him until Policemen Gilligan and Quinn drove them off; Black neighbors were coming out to defend him.

accounts.label: The Sun (New York)
accounts.gist: A dozen white boys at Seventh Avenue and Thirtieth Street harassed a dozen or more Black men with a rope; fifty men and boys chased Jackson with yells of 'lynch him' until he reached Detective Quinn at Thirty-second Street.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff editorial
accounts.gist: A New York fight in which a Black man bested a white man drew a white mob crying 'Lynch the nigger!' before police rescued him; it names no one and may describe another incident.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'Almost a Race Riot' with the deck 'Ruffians Assault Negroes' and called the attackers 'ruffians' throughout.
The Sun's 'Boys Start a Little Race War' cast the episode lightly as boys' mischief while still calling the pursuers 'rowdies' and 'loafers'.
The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic used a New York mob's cry of 'Lynch the nigger!' to mock the North's professed sympathy 'for the negro of the south', without condemning the mob.
